Deleting your account permanently removes the following, and it cannot be recovered.

• All registered pet profiles
• Medical records, appointments, vaccination records
• Health diaries, health metrics, daily care
• Community posts, comments, likes
• Care-sharing relationships

care.guideSource: Source: general Korean vet recommendations · AAFCO/ASPCA guidelines. Reactions vary by individual allergies and constitution, so consult a vet if you notice suspicious symptoms.
care.monthlyDisclaimer: The timing of these cautions can vary by region, temperature, and living environment. Adjust preventive meds, vaccines, and disease management with your vet based on your pet's species, age, and health.
care.seniorDisclaimer: This is general guidance. Consult a vet for an accurate diagnosis.

1.title: Watch for cold-snap exposure
1.body: Long outdoor exposure risks hypothermia, so keep walks short.

1.title: Check for hypothermia signs
1.body: If you see shivering, lethargy, dull responses, or a cold body, move them somewhere warm right away.

1.title: Check frostbite-prone areas
1.body: After walks, check that ear tips, tail, and toes aren't cold or pale.

1.title: Remove de-icer
1.body: After walks, wipe calcium chloride and de-icer off paw pads, between toes, and the belly.

1.title: Care for cracked paw pads
1.body: Winter dryness and de-icer can crack paw pads, so check their moisture.

1.title: Beware heater burns
1.body: Keep distance and limit time near heaters, electric blankets, and heat mats.

1.title: Prevent cord chewing
1.body: Tidy up cords for electric blankets, heaters, and power strips so they can't be chewed.

1.title: Manage indoor humidity
1.body: Heating dries the air and can cause itchy skin, so manage humidity.

1.title: Dry fully after baths
1.body: In winter wet fur can lower body temperature, so dry thoroughly after baths.

1.title: Manage reduced activity
1.body: Shorter walks make weight gain easy, so review food and treat amounts.

1.title: Watch senior pets' joints
1.body: Cold can stiffen joints, so check for limping and stair avoidance.

1.title: No access to antifreeze
1.body: Car coolant and antifreeze can be dangerous even in small amounts, so store sealed.

1.title: Check for cats near cars
1.body: On cold days cats may hide under cars or in engine bays, so check before starting.

1.title: Prepare for power outages
1.body: Keep food, water, meds, a blanket, a carrier, and medical records as an emergency kit.

1.title: Check winter skin condition
1.body: If flaking, dandruff, excessive scratching, or shedding increase, check the skin.

2.title: Prepare for late-winter cold
2.body: Even when it seems milder, sudden cold can return, so keep up warmth care.

2.title: Short, frequent walks
2.body: For small, short-haired, or senior pets, several short walks are safer than one long one.

2.title: Remove de-icer residue
2.body: De-icer can remain on roadsides even after snow melts, so wipe paws.

2.title: Check for snow between toes
2.body: After snowy walks, check that no ice or snowballs are stuck between toes.

2.title: Manage dry skin
2.body: Heating continues, so humidify, brush, and adjust bath intervals.

2.title: Limit direct heater contact
2.body: Even if it doesn't seem hot, prolonged contact can cause low-temperature burns.

2.title: Check senior pets' pain
2.body: Look for stiffness right after waking, jump avoidance, or walk refusal.

2.title: Check weight gain
2.body: If activity dropped over winter, check weight and the waistline.

2.title: Plan spring prevention
2.body: Before it warms up, review tick, flea, and heartworm prevention schedules.

2.title: Check preventive med stock
2.body: Before outdoor activity rises in spring, check you have enough preventive meds.

2.title: Pre-check window screens
2.body: Before opening windows in spring, check screens and loose window frames.

2.title: Store spring-cleaning supplies
2.body: Keep detergents, disinfectants, and air fresheners out of your pet's reach.

2.title: Review allergy history
2.body: If there was dermatitis or extra tearing last spring, get ready to watch again this year.

2.title: Check outing gear
2.body: Before spring outings, check harness, collar, leash, and carrier locks.

2.title: Review checkup schedule
2.body: Before spring activity rises, check teeth, weight, skin, and heartworm test schedules.

3.title: Check tick/flea prevention
3.body: As it warms up and walks increase, exposure to external parasites can rise.

3.title: Check the body after walks
3.body: Check for ticks on ears, neck, armpits, between toes, and around the tail.

3.title: Keep up heartworm prevention
3.body: Prevention matters from around when mosquitoes appear, so don't skip the schedule.

3.title: Watch for pollen allergies
3.body: If paw licking, skin redness, tearing, or ear itching increase, check for allergies.

3.title: Wipe paws after outings
3.body: Wipe paws and belly after walks to reduce pollen, dust, and dirt irritation.

3.title: Check spring-flower toxicity
3.body: When bringing in bouquets or pots, check whether the plants are toxic to pets.

3.title: No lily exposure for cats
3.body: Lilies can be very dangerous to cats, so it's safer not to keep them indoors.

3.title: Beware bulb plants
3.body: Keep bulb plants like tulips and daffodils from being chewed or swallowed.

3.title: Check screens and windows
3.body: As windows get opened more, check for fall risks in advance.

3.title: Beware yard fertilizer
3.body: After using fertilizer, herbicide, or pesticide, let it fully dry before access.

3.title: No eating wild mushrooms
3.body: Mushrooms after rain are hard to judge for toxicity, so prevent eating them.

3.title: Start shedding care
3.body: During spring shedding, brush to reduce matting and skin irritation.

3.title: Check ear odor
3.body: Allergies or humidity changes can cause ear infections, so check odor and scratching.

3.title: Check ID tag
3.body: Before outings increase, check the ID tag, microchip, and contact info.

3.title: Check vaccination schedule
3.body: Before outdoor activity, check rabies, combo vaccine, and deworming schedules.

4.title: Intensive tick checks
4.body: After walks in parks, lawns, or trails, check the whole body carefully.

4.title: Keep up flea prevention
4.body: Warm weather can increase flea activity too, so continue prevention.

4.title: Continue heartworm prevention
4.body: When mosquitoes start appearing, infection risk grows, so keep up prevention.

4.title: Reduce pollen contact
4.body: Wipe fur and paws after walks so pollen doesn't linger on the skin.

4.title: Watch tearing/sneezing
4.body: Check for seasonal tearing, sneezing, or discomfort around the nose.

4.title: Check skin licking
4.body: Excessive paw licking or belly scratching may be an allergic skin issue.

4.title: Limit fertilizer/herbicide exposure
4.body: Let treated flower beds, lawns, and gardens pass the safe interval before access.

4.title: Clear away toxic plants
4.body: Keep risky plants like lilies, tulips, and daffodils out of your pet's reach.

4.title: Carrier practice for outings
4.body: Before trips, get them used to the carrier starting with short sessions.

4.title: Check harness size
4.body: Weight may have changed over winter, so check the harness isn't too tight or loose.

4.title: Car travel safety
4.body: On drives or trips, use a carrier or a seatbelt-type restraint.

4.title: Beware debris on trails
4.body: Check that grass seeds, thorns, or small stones aren't stuck between toes.

4.title: Beware wildlife contact
4.body: Keep them from approaching wildlife droppings or carcasses during outdoor activity.

4.title: Manage indoor pest control
4.body: Keep roach bait, ant bait, and pesticides out of your pet's reach.

4.title: Consider a spring checkup
4.body: Before activity rises, check weight, teeth, skin, and parasite prevention status.

5.title: Adjust to early-summer heat
5.body: A sudden temperature rise can cause heat stress, so adjust walk intensity gradually.

5.title: Reduce midday walks
5.body: Avoid walks during hot hours and add morning or evening walks.

5.title: Beware paw-pad burns
5.body: Asphalt and sand can get hot, so check ground temperature before walks.

5.title: Prepare water and shade
5.body: For outdoor activity, always prepare fresh water and shade to rest in.

5.title: Never leave in the car
5.body: Even briefly, car interior temperature rises fast, so don't leave them alone.

5.title: Check heartworm prevention
5.body: Mosquito activity is increasing, so check that preventive meds are being given.

5.title: Keep checking ticks/fleas
5.body: After walks in grassy areas, check ears, neck, armpits, and between toes.

5.title: Watch early ear-infection signs
5.body: If ear odor, head shaking, or ear scratching increase, check the ears.

5.title: Dry thoroughly after baths
5.body: Staying damp too long can cause dermatitis, so dry fur and paws well.

5.title: Beware over-grooming
5.body: Shaving fur too short can expose skin to UV and heat.

5.title: Check vaccines before travel
5.body: Before boarding, pensions, or daycare, check vaccination and deworming status.

5.title: Manage travel stress
5.body: Before long trips, prepare a carrier, water, pee pads, and their usual food.

5.title: Final spring toxic-plant check
5.body: Double-check that bouquets, pots, and garden plants are safe.

5.title: Check food storage
5.body: Higher temperatures speed food spoilage, so store sealed.

5.title: Watch for skin redness
5.body: Heat plus allergies can increase skin trouble, so check the belly and paws.

6.title: Start heatstroke prevention
6.body: Avoid excessive exercise on hot days and increase indoor rest time.

6.title: Limit midday outings
6.body: Reduce walks and outdoor play when temperature and humidity are high.

6.title: Never leave in a vehicle
6.body: Even with windows cracked, a car interior can get dangerously hot.

6.title: Prevent dehydration
6.body: Check the water bowl often and bring portable water on outings.

6.title: Secure shade
6.body: When staying outdoors, always provide shade away from direct sun.

6.title: Check paw-pad burns
6.body: Roads, decks, and sand heat up easily, so check before walking.

6.title: Beware heat for flat-faced breeds
6.body: Minimize heat exposure for short-nosed breeds like pugs, bulldogs, and shih tzus.

6.title: Care for senior/obese pets
6.body: Senior, obese, or heart/respiratory-condition pets can be more heat-vulnerable.

6.title: Beware rainy-season dermatitis
6.body: Dry wet fur and paws well and check that skin isn't reddened.

6.title: Manage ear infections
6.body: High humidity can increase ear infections, so check ear odor and discharge.

6.title: Keep up heartworm prevention
6.body: Mosquito activity is picking up, so keep prevention consistent.

6.title: Keep up flea/tick prevention
6.body: Continue external parasite prevention and post-walk checks in summer too.

6.title: Beware food/treat spoilage
6.body: Don't leave food and treats in hot, humid spots; store them sealed.

6.title: Check safety before water play
6.body: Even strong swimmers need a life vest and supervision.

6.title: Prepare for heavy rain
6.body: For outages or flooding, prepare food, meds, water, and a carrier.

7.title: Peak heatwave heatstroke alert
7.body: Excessive panting, drooling, staggering, and vomiting should be treated as emergency signs.

7.title: Strictly adjust walk times
7.body: Move walks to early morning or after sunset.

7.title: No leaving in the car
7.body: In summer a car interior heats up very fast, so never leave them alone.

7.title: Manage indoor temperature
7.body: Indoors that are too hot or poorly ventilated can cause heat stress.

7.title: Always provide fresh water
7.body: Place water bowls in several spots and refill often.

7.title: Beware paw-pad burns
7.body: Road heat can linger after sunset, so check ground temperature.

7.title: Beware drowning during water play
7.body: At pools, valleys, and the sea, provide supervision and a life vest.

7.title: No contact with algae water
7.body: Keep them from drinking or entering water that looks odd or smells.

7.title: Beware mold after the rainy season
7.body: Wash and dry damp bedding and toys to reduce mold exposure.

7.title: Dry ears and between toes
7.body: After water play and baths, dry ears and between toes well.

7.title: Check summer skin trouble
7.body: Check that the belly, armpits, and groin aren't red or damp.

7.title: Keep up heartworm prevention
7.body: It's a high-mosquito-exposure period, so don't miss prevention.

7.title: Check insect bites
7.body: After walks, check the face, paws, and belly for swelling or itching.

7.title: Manage vacation travel stress
7.body: After long trips, check for appetite loss, diarrhea, vomiting, and lethargy.

7.title: Manage summer food waste
7.body: Close the trash bin to prevent eating spoiled food, bones, or packaging.

8.title: Manage sustained heat
8.body: Accumulated heat can sap stamina, so reduce outings and exercise.

8.title: Watch dehydration signs
8.body: Suspect dehydration if gums are sticky, they're lethargic, or urine output drops.

8.title: Check ground before walks
8.body: Hot roads, sand, or decks risk paw-pad burns.

8.title: Cool the car before travel
8.body: Lower the interior temperature before loading them and keep airflow during travel.

8.title: Beware direct AC airflow
8.body: Adjust their spot so AC airflow doesn't constantly hit the body.

8.title: Manage indoor-outdoor temp gap
8.body: Prevent condition drops from sudden temperature changes.

8.title: Check skin after water play
8.body: After swimming, check for skin redness, ear odor, and dampness between toes.

8.title: Beware algae/polluted water
8.body: Check lake or river water in summer and block access if it looks off.

8.title: Continue heartworm prevention
8.body: Mosquito exposure continues, so keep the prevention schedule.

8.title: Keep checking ticks/fleas
8.body: Check the whole body after walks in grass and vacation spots.

8.title: Beware food spoilage
8.body: Don't leave the food bag open long; store in a cool, dry place.

8.title: Watch eczema/hot spots
8.body: If they keep licking one area or fur stays wet, check for dermatitis.

8.title: Beware bee/insect stings
8.body: If the face or mouth suddenly swells or breathing is labored, seek care immediately.

8.title: Watch post-vacation recovery
8.body: After trips, check for diarrhea, vomiting, appetite loss, or excessive fatigue.

8.title: Prepare for typhoons
8.body: For outages and outing limits, prepare food, water, meds, and toilet supplies.

9.title: Beware late-summer heat
9.body: Daytime can still be hot in September, so avoid midday walks.

9.title: Keep up tick prevention
9.body: Even as it cools, tick activity can continue, so keep prevention going.

9.title: Check the body after walks
9.body: After grass or fallen-leaf areas, check ears, armpits, and between toes.

9.title: Keep up heartworm prevention
9.body: Continue prevention until mosquitoes are completely gone.

9.title: Watch condition with temp swings
9.body: Check for coughing, lethargy, or appetite changes from day-night temp gaps.

9.title: Start of fall shedding
9.body: Brush to reduce matting, skin irritation, and hairball risk in cats.

9.title: Watch the switch to dry skin
9.body: Even after summer eczema, fall dryness can cause itching.

9.title: Check walking gear
9.body: Before outings rise, check harness, leash, and collar wear.

9.title: Check grass seeds/debris
9.body: Look for grass seeds or thorns stuck between toes, around ears, or on the belly.

9.title: Start beware of wild mushrooms
9.body: Keep them from eating mushrooms that appear on trails after rain.

9.title: Beware rodenticide access
9.body: Keep indoor/outdoor pest-control chemicals out of your pet's reach.

9.title: Check ID tag for fall outings
9.body: As outings increase, check the ID tag and contact info.

9.title: Watch allergy recurrence
9.body: Fall pollen or mold can bring back skin and ear problems.

9.title: Pace increased activity
9.body: Suddenly increasing exercise just because it's cooler can strain the joints.

9.title: Consider a fall checkup
9.body: Check weight, skin, teeth, and heartworm status that changed over summer.

10.title: Late-stage tick care
10.body: Fall walks increase, so keep up prevention and body checks.

10.title: Beware debris in leaves
10.body: Insects, glass shards, or food waste can lurk under fallen leaves.

10.title: No eating wild mushrooms
10.body: Mushrooms grow a lot in fall, so keep them from eating any on walks.

10.title: No access to rodenticide
10.body: Store pest-control chemicals where pets can't reach them.

10.title: Beware chocolate
10.body: Chocolate exposure can rise during Halloween or treat season.

10.title: Beware xylitol
10.body: Sugar-free gum, candy, and some desserts can be dangerous to pets.

10.title: Check costume stress
10.body: If a costume blocks breathing, walking, or vision, take it off right away.

10.title: Beware decoration chewing
10.body: Keep small ornaments, strings, ribbons, and plastic pieces from being swallowed.

10.title: Manage visitor stress
10.body: On days with doorbells, strangers, and noise, set up a quiet space.

10.title: Prevent door-dash escapes
10.body: On days with visitors coming and going, limit access to the entrance.

10.title: Watch senior pets' joints
10.body: In cool weather, check if movement slows or they avoid stairs.

10.title: Keep up shedding care
10.body: Brush to reduce matting and skin irritation.

10.title: Start preparing for indoor dryness
10.body: Before switching on heating, check water intake and skin condition.

10.title: Pace activity changes
10.body: Suddenly running long in cool weather can strain muscles and joints.

10.title: Manage increased fall appetite
10.body: Even if appetite rises, keep treat and food amounts steady.

11.title: Consider a pre-winter checkup
11.body: Before the cold, check teeth, weight, joints, heart, and kidneys.

11.title: Inspect heaters before use
11.body: Check cords and overheating risk on heaters, electric blankets, and heat mats.

11.title: Prevent low-temperature burns
11.body: Adjust usage time so they don't lean against heaters while sleeping.

11.title: Start managing indoor humidity
11.body: Once heating starts, skin and the respiratory tract can get dry.

11.title: Step up drying after baths
11.body: As it gets colder, dry fur thoroughly after baths.

11.title: Prepare warm walk gear
11.body: Consider warm clothing for small, short-haired, or senior pets.

11.title: Prepare paw protection
11.body: Check paw condition in advance for winter de-icer and cold ground.

11.title: Prepare for reduced activity
11.body: Before walks drop due to cold, plan indoor play and weight management.

11.title: Beware holiday/gathering food
11.body: Don't feed onions, garlic, bones, greasy food, or raw dough.

11.title: Manage the food-waste bin
11.body: After gatherings, close the lid to prevent eating bones, packaging, or spoiled food.

11.title: Manage chocolate/desserts
11.body: Before year-end gifts and treats increase, store risky foods separately.

11.title: Prepare a winter go-bag
11.body: Keep food, water, meds, a blanket, a carrier, and medical records ready.

11.title: Manage car antifreeze
11.body: After winter car maintenance, check that coolant and antifreeze aren't leaking.

11.title: Watch senior pets' pain
11.body: Cold can worsen joint pain, so watch for gait changes.

11.title: Adjust the winter walk routine
11.body: On days with sharp temperature drops, reduce walk time and intensity.

12.title: Beware the full cold snap
12.body: On cold days, reduce outdoor time and prioritize indoor rest.

12.title: Check for hypothermia signs
12.body: If you see shivering, lethargy, dull responses, or a cold body, warm them immediately.

12.title: Check frostbite areas
12.body: After walks, check that ear tips, tail, and toes aren't cold or pale.

12.title: Remove de-icer/calcium chloride
12.body: After walks, wipe paws and belly to reduce skin irritation and ingestion risk.

12.title: Beware slipping on snow
12.body: On icy roads, joints and ligaments can be strained, so walk slowly.

12.title: Prevent heater burns
12.body: Keep them from prolonged contact with heaters, electric blankets, and hot packs.

12.title: Prevent cord chewing
12.body: Tidy up cords for tree lights, heaters, and electric blankets so they can't be chewed.

12.title: Beware Christmas-decoration ingestion
12.body: Ribbons, tinsel, and glass ornaments can be dangerous if swallowed.

12.title: Manage candle/fire risk
12.body: Limit use of candles and incense so they aren't knocked over or touch fur.

12.title: No sharing year-end food
12.body: Don't feed chocolate, alcohol, greasy meat, bones, or xylitol foods.

12.title: Manage visitor stress
12.body: On busy guest days, set aside a quiet space to rest.

12.title: Prevent door-dash escapes
12.body: At year-end gatherings the front door opens often, so check ID tags and a separate space.

12.title: No access to antifreeze
12.body: Store car coolant and antifreeze where pets can't reach them.

12.title: Prepare for outages/cold
12.body: Prepare food, water, meds, a blanket, a carrier, and medical records as an emergency kit.

12.title: Manage winter weight
12.body: Reduced activity makes weight gain easy, so review food and treat amounts.

SENIOR.title: From age 7, it's time to start regular checkups
SENIOR.body: To catch silent kidney, liver, and heart disease early, get regular blood and urine tests. Joint pain also starts to show signs.
watchFor: Excessive sleep, not hearing when called (cataracts/hearing)
Changes in gum color or breath odor

GERIATRIC.title: In old age, don't let even small changes slip by
GERIATRIC.body: Kidney failure, heart disease, and tumors become more likely. Check up every 6 months; a low-protein, low-phosphorus prescription diet may need consideration.
GERIATRIC.checkupCadence: Full checkup every 6 months + quarterly weigh-ins
watchFor: Appetite or weight loss lasting over a week
Worsening breath odor and reddened gums

SENIOR.title: Cats hide illness well
SENIOR.body: From age 7, chronic kidney disease (CKD), hyperthyroidism, and diabetes become common. Regular blood and urine tests are key to not miss quiet changes.
watchFor: Drinking more or using the litter box more often
Gradual weight loss while appetite stays similar

GERIATRIC.title: Weigh senior cats every quarter
GERIATRIC.body: A loss of more than 5% of body weight is a meaningful sign. Kidney failure, thyroid issues, and tumors can all show weight loss as the first clue.
GERIATRIC.checkupCadence: Full checkup every 6 months + monthly weigh-ins
watchFor: Appetite or weight loss lasting over a week
Worsening breath odor and reddened gums

SENIOR.title: Birds barely show when they're sick
SENIOR.body: Changes in feathers, posture, and digestion are almost the only signs. If they doze with puffed-up posture or eat less, see a vet immediately.
SENIOR.checkupCadence: Annual visit to an avian specialist

SENIOR.title: For reptiles, environment management is medicine
SENIOR.body: Checking temperature, humidity, and UVB lighting is the core of daily care. Keep consistent records of appetite and shedding cycles.
SENIOR.checkupCadence: Annual visit to an exotic-animal specialist

SENIOR.title: Small animals change fast
SENIOR.body: Hamsters and guinea pigs age quickly, so daily weight and food-intake checks help. Take even small changes to a vet quickly.
watchFor: Huddling in a corner, less movement

SENIOR.title: As they age, shorten the checkup interval
SENIOR.body: It varies by species, but at least an annual checkup is recommended after entering the senior stage.

BIRD.headline: Vets that treat birds are limited
BIRD.body: General vets often can't treat birds. Find an avian or exotic-animal hospital in advance.

REPTILE.headline: Reptiles & amphibians need an exotic vet
REPTILE.body: General clinics may refuse care or struggle to dose meds. Search for exotic-animal specialists first.

SMALL_ANIMAL.headline: Hamsters, guinea pigs & rabbits are safer at a specialist
SMALL_ANIMAL.body: Small animals react strongly to meds, so a specialist's experience matters more than general care.

OTHER.headline: Find an exotic-animal specialist in advance
OTHER.body: General vets may not be able to treat them. Knowing a species-appropriate specialist in advance saves time in an emergency.

HEATWAVE.title: Watch for heatstroke signs
HEATWAVE.body: Excessive panting, drooling, staggering, vomiting, and lethargy can signal heatstroke — move them to a cool place immediately.
HEATWAVE.caution: Watch flat-faced, senior, obese, and heart/respiratory-condition animals

HEATWAVE.title: Stop midday walks
HEATWAVE.body: Avoid walks and vigorous play during hot hours; move briefly in the early morning or after sunset.
HEATWAVE.caution: Watch large dogs, thick coats, and high-energy breeds

HEATWAVE.title: Check paw-pad burns
HEATWAVE.body: Hot asphalt, decks, and sand can burn paw pads — check the ground temperature before walks.
HEATWAVE.caution: Watch small dogs, short-legged breeds, and animals with sensitive pads

HEATWAVE.title: Never leave in a vehicle
HEATWAVE.body: Car interior temperature rises fast even briefly, so never leave your pet alone.
HEATWAVE.caution: All animals, especially cats and small dogs during transport

HEATWAVE.title: Secure water and shade
HEATWAVE.body: Bring fresh water on outings and let them rest in shade often to prevent overheating.
HEATWAVE.caution: Watch young, senior, and dehydration-prone animals

COLDWAVE.title: Shorten walk time
COLDWAVE.body: On days with low wind chill, favor short, safe potty walks over long ones.
COLDWAVE.caution: Watch small dogs, short-haired, senior, and young animals

COLDWAVE.title: Check for hypothermia signs
COLDWAVE.body: If you see shivering, lethargy, dull responses, or a cold body, move them indoors and warm them right away.
COLDWAVE.caution: Watch senior, condition-having, and lean animals

COLDWAVE.title: Check paws and ear tips
COLDWAVE.body: After walks, check that ear tips, tail, and toes aren't cold or pale.
COLDWAVE.caution: Watch thin-eared breeds, short-haired, and outdoor animals

COLDWAVE.title: Wipe off de-icer
COLDWAVE.body: After walks, thoroughly wipe calcium chloride, de-icer, and snow off paw pads and between toes.
COLDWAVE.caution: Watch animals that lick their paws

COLDWAVE.title: Dry wet fur immediately
COLDWAVE.body: Fur wet from snow or rain can lower body temperature, so dry ears, belly, and paws thoroughly.
COLDWAVE.caution: Watch long-haired, double-coated, and skin-condition animals

RAIN_HEAVY.title: Limit outings
RAIN_HEAVY.body: On heavy-rain days, avoid walks and outdoor activity; use indoor potty or play instead if possible.
RAIN_HEAVY.caution: Watch small dogs, senior dogs, and timid animals

RAIN_HEAVY.title: No access to flooded areas
RAIN_HEAVY.body: Keep them from flooded roads, riverbanks, and underpasses due to slipping and contaminated-water risks.
RAIN_HEAVY.caution: Watch small dogs, senior dogs, and low-vantage animals

RAIN_HEAVY.title: No drinking standing water
RAIN_HEAVY.body: Puddles, rainwater, and river water may be contaminated, so prevent drinking or licking.
RAIN_HEAVY.caution: Watch dogs that drink readily on walks

RAIN_HEAVY.title: Beware drains and manholes
RAIN_HEAVY.body: If you must go out, avoid fast-draining gutters, manholes, and slopes, and use a short leash.

RAIN_HEAVY.title: Prepare for emergency evacuation
RAIN_HEAVY.body: If flooding is possible, keep a carrier, leash, meds, food, water, and medical records ready to grab.

DUST_PM.title: Reduce outdoor activity
DUST_PM.body: On bad fine-dust days, cut long walks and running, and use indoor play instead.

DUST_PM.title: Keep walks short
DUST_PM.body: If a potty break is needed, keep it short and avoid main roads and construction areas.
DUST_PM.caution: Watch flat-faced, senior, and weak-airway animals

DUST_PM.title: Wipe fur after outings
DUST_PM.body: After walks, wipe paws, face, and coat so dust doesn't linger on skin and around the eyes.

DUST_PM.title: Watch breathing changes
DUST_PM.body: If you see coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath, or eye/nose irritation, rest indoors and check.
DUST_PM.caution: Watch asthma, heart disease, and tracheal-collapse history

DUST_PM.title: Manage indoor air
DUST_PM.body: Don't leave windows open long; use an air purifier or time ventilation to reduce indoor dust.
DUST_PM.caution: Watch young, senior, and pregnant animals

YELLOW_DUST.title: Minimize dust exposure
YELLOW_DUST.body: During a yellow-dust advisory, reduce walks and outdoor play and use indoor activity instead.
YELLOW_DUST.caution: Watch respiratory-condition, senior, and young animals

YELLOW_DUST.title: Check eye/nose irritation
YELLOW_DUST.body: If eye discharge, tearing, sneezing, or nose-rubbing increase, watch for dust irritation.
YELLOW_DUST.caution: Watch flat-faced, bulgy-eyed breeds, and conjunctivitis history

YELLOW_DUST.title: Wipe the whole body after walks
YELLOW_DUST.body: After outings, wipe paws, belly, face, and coat so dust doesn't remain.
YELLOW_DUST.caution: Watch long-haired animals and frequently-grooming cats

YELLOW_DUST.title: Keep water bowls clean
YELLOW_DUST.body: Dust can get indoors, so rinse bowls and dishes often and provide clean water.

YELLOW_DUST.title: Limit window opening
YELLOW_DUST.body: Close windows during heavy dust and ventilate briefly when levels drop.
YELLOW_DUST.caution: Watch asthma, bronchitis, and heart-disease animals

THUNDER.title: Set up a safe indoor space
THUNDER.body: Before thunder starts, prepare a quiet room away from windows or a spot near the carrier.

THUNDER.title: Don't force them out
THUNDER.body: Don't block hiding behavior; if the spot is safe, give them time to calm down on their own.
THUNDER.caution: Watch timid cats and rescue animals

THUNDER.title: Prevent escape
THUNDER.body: They may bolt outside startled by thunder, so close the entrance, windows, and screens.
THUNDER.caution: Watch animals with a history of running off on walks

THUNDER.title: Buffer the noise
THUNDER.body: Draw curtains and soften outside sound with TV, radio, or white noise.
THUNDER.caution: Watch noise-sensitive animals and senior dogs

THUNDER.title: Stop walks immediately
THUNDER.body: With a lightning forecast or thunderstorm, stop outdoor walks, parks, and riverside activity and head indoors.
THUNDER.caution: Outdoor-only-potty animals should use a short, safe spot

RAIN_LIGHT.title: Keep potty outings short
RAIN_LIGHT.body: On light-rain days, keep only essential potty outings short and dry wet fur right away.
RAIN_LIGHT.caution: Watch small dogs, short-haired, and senior animals

RAIN_LIGHT.title: Wipe wet paws right away
RAIN_LIGHT.body: After outings, wipe and dry paw pads and between toes to reduce moisture and skin irritation.

RAIN_LIGHT.title: Prevent rainwater drinking
RAIN_LIGHT.body: Roadside puddles and rainwater may be contaminated, so prevent drinking or licking.

RAIN_LIGHT.title: Check raincoat/boot discomfort
RAIN_LIGHT.body: If a raincoat or boots hinder walking, pottying, or breathing, reduce wear time or avoid them.
RAIN_LIGHT.caution: Watch animals that dislike wearing clothes

RAIN_LIGHT.title: Dry ears and belly
RAIN_LIGHT.body: After getting rained on, dry around the ears, belly, and inner legs well to prevent skin and ear issues.
RAIN_LIGHT.caution: Watch floppy-eared breeds, long-haired, and ear-infection history

TEMP_DIFF.title: Adjust outing times
TEMP_DIFF.body: If mornings and evenings are cold, shift walks toward midday or bring warmth.
TEMP_DIFF.caution: Watch senior, short-haired, and small dogs

TEMP_DIFF.title: Watch cough/runny nose
TEMP_DIFF.body: On days with big temperature swings, check for coughing, runny nose, sneezing, or appetite loss.
TEMP_DIFF.caution: Watch weak-airway animals and flat-faced breeds

TEMP_DIFF.title: Check joint stiffness
TEMP_DIFF.body: After temperature changes, if there's limping or stair/jump avoidance, lower activity intensity.
TEMP_DIFF.caution: Watch senior dogs, arthritis, and patella history

TEMP_DIFF.title: Reduce sudden indoor temp swings
TEMP_DIFF.body: Rather than blasting heat/AC suddenly, adjust the indoor-outdoor gap gradually.

TEMP_DIFF.title: Increase walk intensity slowly
TEMP_DIFF.body: Don't suddenly run long just because it's cooler — increase walk time and exercise gradually.
TEMP_DIFF.caution: Watch obese, senior, and under-exercised animals

HUMIDITY_HIGH.title: Beware poor heat release
HUMIDITY_HIGH.body: High humidity makes it hard to cool down by panting, so reduce exercise.
HUMIDITY_HIGH.caution: Watch flat-faced, obese, and senior animals

HUMIDITY_HIGH.title: Check skin eczema
HUMIDITY_HIGH.body: Check that the belly, armpits, groin, and between toes aren't red or damp.
HUMIDITY_HIGH.caution: Watch long-haired animals and dermatitis history

HUMIDITY_HIGH.title: Keep ears dry
HUMIDITY_HIGH.body: After baths, rain, or water play, dry the inner ear and around it well to lower ear-infection risk.
HUMIDITY_HIGH.caution: Watch floppy-eared breeds and frequent swimmers

HUMIDITY_HIGH.title: Dry bedding and toys
HUMIDITY_HIGH.body: Wash and fully dry damp bedding and toys to reduce mold and odor.

HUMIDITY_HIGH.title: Beware food spoilage
HUMIDITY_HIGH.body: On hot, humid days, store food and treats sealed; don't feed if the smell or color changes.

HUMIDITY_LOW.title: Check skin flaking
HUMIDITY_LOW.body: If dandruff, flaking, dull fur, or excessive scratching increase, check for dry skin.
HUMIDITY_LOW.caution: Watch skin-condition history, short-haired, and senior animals

HUMIDITY_LOW.title: Add indoor humidity
HUMIDITY_LOW.body: If the air is dry, keep the indoor environment comfortable with humidifying and bowl management.

HUMIDITY_LOW.title: Avoid over-bathing
HUMIDITY_LOW.body: Frequent baths can strip skin oils, so review bath intervals and shampoo irritation.

HUMIDITY_LOW.title: Check cracked paw pads
HUMIDITY_LOW.body: If pads are rough or cracked, check after walks and give the needed moisturizing care.
HUMIDITY_LOW.caution: Watch dogs that walk a lot in winter

HUMIDITY_LOW.title: Reduce static stress
HUMIDITY_LOW.body: On dry days static can build up in blankets and fur, so combine brushing with humidity care.

UV_HIGH.title: Avoid midday sun
UV_HIGH.body: On high-UV days, avoid walks from 10am to 3pm and stick to shade.
UV_HIGH.caution: Watch white-coated, short-haired, and thin-skinned animals

UV_HIGH.title: Protect ears/nose/belly
UV_HIGH.body: Sparsely furred ear tips, nose area, and belly can be sun-sensitive, so reduce exposure time.
UV_HIGH.caution: Watch white cats, short-haired, and recently-groomed animals

UV_HIGH.title: Beware over-grooming
UV_HIGH.body: Shaving fur too short can expose skin directly to UV and heat — be careful.

UV_HIGH.title: Choose shaded walks
UV_HIGH.body: If a walk is needed, choose shaded paths, dirt, or grass, and reduce waiting in the sun.
UV_HIGH.caution: Watch sensitive-pad animals and senior dogs

UV_HIGH.title: Consult on pet sunscreen
UV_HIGH.body: If some areas are sun-sensitive, don't use human products freely — consult a vet about pet-specific ones.
UV_HIGH.caution: Watch skin-condition, allergy, and licking-habit animals

WIND_STRONG.title: Limit outdoor walks
WIND_STRONG.body: Strong wind brings flying objects, noise, and sudden direction changes, so reduce walks.
WIND_STRONG.caution: Watch small dogs, timid animals, and senior animals

WIND_STRONG.title: Use a short leash
WIND_STRONG.body: If you must go out, use a short leash and a well-fitting harness to prevent sudden bolting.
WIND_STRONG.caution: Watch escape history and harness-slip history

WIND_STRONG.title: Check windows and screens
WIND_STRONG.body: In strong wind, rattling windows and screens risk falls or escape, so close them.
WIND_STRONG.caution: Watch cats and animals that climb to windowsills

WIND_STRONG.title: No access to falling objects
WIND_STRONG.body: Signs, branches, and construction areas risk falling objects, so keep them away.
WIND_STRONG.caution: Watch when the walk route is downtown or near construction

WIND_STRONG.title: Ease noise stress
WIND_STRONG.body: If wind sounds cause anxiety, provide calm with a quiet room, blanket, and white noise.
WIND_STRONG.caution: Watch noise-phobia, separation-anxiety, and senior dogs
